The keys of a `run: proxy` step, one paragraph each: `url` and its path values, `path_slashes`, `method`, `headers` and `auth`, `content_types`, `max_bytes`, `timeout`, `disposition` and `filename`, `cache_control`.

`url` (required): the upstream URL. The scheme and host must be literal text or an env value (`${{ env.API_BASE }}/v1/...`); request input and step outputs may fill path segments and query values only, after a literal `/`, `?` or `#`, and are encoded for where they land (a value cannot add a parameter, and a path value is one plain segment: see Path values). Any other reference before the path, or a `:name` placeholder there, is refused when the file is written and when the step runs - tainted or not, so a URL stored in a table or returned by an earlier step cannot be proxied.

Path values: every value placed in the path that you did not write as literal text or an env value must be one plain segment: request input, a stored row (a user may have written it through auto-CRUD), a step output, a set value. A value holding `/` or `\`, also percent-encoded once or more (`%2F`, `%5C`, `%252F`), or that is `.` or `..` (also encoded), fails the step before the call (`proxy url: ... one path segment only`): an upstream that decodes %2F and then normalizes its path would turn `..%2Fadmin` into a call to another endpoint with your credentials. So a stored `remote_slug` of `../bytes/64` fails the step, and a stored file key `users/42/a.png` fails it unless the step sets `path_slashes: true`. Pass such a value as a query value instead (`?file=${{ params.file }}`); query values are unaffected. Literal text and env values in the path are yours and are sent as written.

`path_slashes`: optional, a literal `true` or `false` (default false). `true` lets a path value that is not request text span segments: a SQL row (also one looked up by a request id, `WHERE id = :id`), an api or compute output, so a stored key `users/42/a.png` goes out as `/files/users/42/a.png`, each segment escaped (`a b` is `a%20b`). An empty segment (a leading, trailing or doubled `/`), a `.` or `..` segment, a `\` and an encoded `/` or `\` still fail the step. Request text (`${{ params.x }}`, a `:name` parameter, a set value or parse output built from the request) always stays one plain segment. The value can name any file under the URL's literal path prefix on your upstream, so set it only when a caller may fetch any such file the flow's own checks allow.

`method`: GET (default) or POST, written literally. A body (`json:` a map, list or one `${{ }}` reference, or `body:` text) needs POST. An upstream POST needs a flow with `method: POST`, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, refused when written and when run in a GET flow: a GET skips the CSRF check, so a link or image on another site could make a signed-in user's browser trigger your (often billable) upstream call.

`headers` and `auth`: the only request headers sent upstream; put credentials in env (`${{ env.KEY }}`). The caller's cookies, Authorization and other headers are never forwarded. Accept-Encoding, Range, If-Range, Host, Content-Length and hop-by-hop headers are refused; a method-override header must be literal or env.

`content_types` (required): the media types the step serves, a subset of the framework list: image/png, image/jpeg, image/gif, image/webp, image/avif, audio/mpeg, audio/mp4, audio/aac, audio/ogg, audio/wav, audio/webm, audio/flac, video/mp4, video/webm, video/ogg, application/pdf, text/csv, application/zip. Never HTML, JavaScript, SVG, XML or JSON.

`max_bytes`: the body cap, bytes or a size (`512KB`, `20MB`; KB and MB are 1024-based). Default 10 MiB, at most 100 MiB. It counts the bytes the caller gets: the client asks the upstream for gzip and decodes it, so a gzip answer is measured decoded.

`timeout`: under `with:` or at the step root, 1s up to the flow time limit's maximum (95 s hosted); default 30s. The call and the whole copy also end at the flow's `on.request.timeout` and when the caller disconnects; only the step's own timeout counts against the host's circuit breaker (api(at:"flows") → circuit_breaker).

`disposition`: `inline` (default) or `attachment`, literal. PDF, CSV and ZIP are always attachments. `filename`: an optional download name (may be a `${{ }}` template); it is cut to its last path part and to letters, digits, space, dot, dash and underscore (others become `_`), at most 128 characters. Its extension always matches the type served: an extension outside that type's set is replaced and a name without one gets it (`report.bat` served as text/csv is sent as `report.csv`, `invoice` as application/pdf as `invoice.pdf`), so request input can name the file but never make it a `.bat`, `.html` or `.svg`. Extensions: png; jpg/jpeg; gif; webp; avif; mp3 (audio/mpeg); m4a/mp4 (audio/mp4); aac; ogg/oga/opus; wav; weba/webm (audio/webm); flac; mp4/m4v (video/mp4); webm; ogv/ogg (video/ogg); pdf; csv; zip. The first listed is the one added.

`cache_control`: optional, literal text: the Cache-Control the answer carries. Without it every proxied answer is `private, no-store`. Directives: public, private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=N, s-maxage=N, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, immutable, no-transform, stale-while-revalidate=N, stale-if-error=N; no `${{ }}` reference and no `private="field"` form. A value a shared cache may store (one without `private` or `no-store`: `public, max-age=300`, `s-maxage=600`) is accepted only on an `auth: none` (or unset) flow with no role or permissions; on any other flow write a private form (`private, max-age=300`), and the write gate refuses the rest. A signed-in caller of a public flow still gets `private, no-store`. Opt in only for an answer that is the same for every caller of the exact URL and may outlive revocation: a shared cache keys by URL alone, so a flow that checks a token, header or cookie outside the URL would serve the cached bytes to anyone, and a revoked share link keeps serving until max-age runs out. On the hosted platform, Cloudflare's default does not store a `/api/...` proxy answer marked `public, max-age=60` (`cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC` on every request), so the header reaches browsers and any other shared cache between the caller and the app, and every request still runs the flow and the upstream call; Cloudflare's default does store a URL that ends in a static file extension (`.png`, `.mp3`, `.pdf`, ...), so do not rely on either behavior: rate_limit bounds upstream calls.
